opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing for us right now is to stay clear about what actually creates long-term value. For a company like Moonshot, the core is the model capability itself. If the model keeps getting meaningfully better, at reasoning, at long context, at actually completing tasks for people, then commercialization becomes much more natural. If the model doesn't improve, then whatever business model you design is built on sand.

So in terms of priorities, I'd put technology first, product and user value second, and monetization third. That doesn't mean monetization is unimportant. It means it should be a result of the first two rather than something that distorts them. There was a period when the whole industry was spending heavily on user acquisition, and we learned some lessons from that. Growth you buy without real retention doesn't compound. What compounds is when the product genuinely solves a problem and people come back because it's useful.

On the business model itself, I see a few layers. One is the consumer side, where people use Kimi as a productivity tool, for research, reading, writing, and increasingly for agent-style tasks where the model goes and does multi-step work on your behalf. As the model takes on more of the real work, people are much more willing to pay, because you're not paying for a chatbot, you're paying for work getting done. That's where I think subscription and usage-based models start to make real sense.

The second layer is developers and enterprises through the API and open models. Open-sourcing strong models has been important for us. It builds trust, it builds an ecosystem, and frankly it pushes us to be honest about where our capability really stands, because everyone can test it.

Underneath all of this is a simple belief: the ceiling of the business is set by the ceiling of intelligence. So the most important commercial decision we make is actually how we allocate compute and talent toward making the next model better. Everything else follows from that.

r001.rationale: The response makes improving model capability the top priority, saying technology comes first and that the key commercial decision is investing in the next model.

r002.rationale: It says meaningful model improvements can make commercialization more natural, but does not state that model leadership in particular areas creates those opportunities.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think about commercialization less as a separate department problem and more as a question of what kind of company we want to be in five or ten years.

If you look at the history of the internet, the biggest companies didn't win because they had the best monetization on day one. They won because they found a product that people genuinely loved, and then the business followed. For Kimi, the first priority has always been that: can we build something that users come back to because it actually makes them smarter or saves them real time? If the answer is yes, there are many ways to make money. If the answer is no, there's no business model that saves you.

That said, I don't think the consumer internet playbook applies one-to-one. A chatbot costs real compute every time someone uses it. So the question isn't just "does it have users," it's "does the value created per interaction exceed the cost of creating it, and is the gap widening over time?" What's encouraging is that the cost curve is falling very fast, and the value per interaction keeps going up as the models get more capable. Two years ago the model could help you summarize a document. Now it can do a meaningful piece of work for you. That changes the economics completely.

So our priorities, in order, are something like this. First, keep pushing the frontier of the model itself, because that's the only real moat in this industry. If you're not at the frontier, you're competing on distribution and price, and that's a game where the big incumbents will always have an advantage. Second, build products where the model's intelligence is the product, not a feature bolted onto something else. Third, and only then, figure out which users are willing to pay. We already see that people doing serious work, developers, researchers, knowledge workers, have a very clear willingness to pay when the model actually delivers. That's a very different signal from advertising-driven consumer growth.

I'd also say we've deliberately not chased every possible revenue line. There was a period in China where the pressure was to spend heavily on user acquisition. We tried some of that, and I think we learned that burning money to buy users who don't stay isn't building a company. It's renting attention. We'd rather be a smaller company that's at the frontier than a large company that's a commodity.

On the API and enterprise side, we're pragmatic. If a business can build something valuable on top of our models, that's a healthy revenue source and it also teaches us what the model is actually good at in the real world. But I'm cautious about becoming a customization shop. The moment you spend most of your energy on bespoke deployments, you stop being an AI company and become a consulting company.

So if I had to compress it: be at the frontier, build products that are the intelligence itself, and let monetization come from the people who get the most value. I think that order matters more than any specific pricing decision.

r001.rationale: The response names pushing the model frontier as the first priority, clearly identifying model improvement as the primary objective.

r002.rationale: The response connects frontier models with a competitive moat and says capable models can support paid products, but it does not state that leadership in particular areas creates commercialization opportunities.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point is that we have to create real value for users. For Kimi, that means continuing to improve the model and turning those capabilities into a product that people find useful enough to come back to. Commercialization has to follow from that value.

There are different ways to capture it, whether through paid features or providing model capabilities through an API. But I wouldn’t treat choosing a revenue model as the first priority. The more important questions are: What can we help users accomplish? How well can we do it? And can we deliver that sustainably, given the cost of inference?

So I’d think about capability, product experience, and commercialization together. We need to learn what people are willing to pay for, while continuing to invest in the technology that makes the product valuable in the first place.

r001.rationale: It frames continuing to improve Kimi’s model as the starting point for creating user value and says commercialization should follow from that value.

r002.rationale: It discusses improving capabilities and learning what users will pay for, but does not say that model leadership in particular areas creates commercialization opportunities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the starting point is whether we’re creating enough value for users. If Kimi can help someone solve a difficult problem or get meaningful work done, then there’s a basis for commercialization. We need to understand which kinds of value people are willing to pay for, and make sure the product delivers that value consistently.

There are different possibilities, including subscriptions and API services. But I wouldn’t treat choosing a payment model as the most important decision. The priority is improving the model’s capabilities and translating those capabilities into a product people want to keep using. Commercialization should grow alongside that, with attention to the cost of serving users and whether the business can be sustainable.

r001.rationale: It calls improving the model’s capabilities the priority, making that the primary current objective.

r002.rationale: It links user value and product capabilities to commercialization, but does not say that model leadership in particular areas creates commercialization opportunities.
